name: Seizure Prediction
title: Seizure Prediction
answer: Seizure prediction is the use of machine learning to forecast epileptic seizures before clinical onset, typically from continuous electroencephalography or wearable signals. It sits within neuroinformatics as a decision support problem rather than a diagnostic one, aiming to give patients and caregivers warning windows. The field covers focal and generalized epilepsies, with models trained on long term recordings from epilepsy monitoring units and ambulatory devices. Unlike seizure detection, which flags events as they happen, prediction tries to identify a preictal state minutes to hours ahead.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Seizure prediction is the use of machine learning to forecast epileptic seizures before clinical onset, typically from continuous electroencephalography or wearable signals. It sits within neuroinformatics as a decision support problem rather than a diagnostic one, aiming to give patients and caregivers warning windows. The field covers focal and generalized epilepsies, with models trained on long term recordings from epilepsy monitoring units and ambulatory devices. Unlike seizure detection, which flags events as they happen, prediction tries to identify a preictal state minutes to hours ahead.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most research models run on retrospective EEG datasets stored in formats such as EDF and processed on standard GPU workstations or cloud instances. Clinical prototypes often use low power wearable or implantable devices that stream reduced channel data to a phone or bedside unit. Training pipelines rely on Python libraries for signal processing and deep learning, with feature extraction sometimes done on device to limit data transfer. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and seizure prediction accounts for a small but active subset of that inventory.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work typically begins by segmenting EEG into interictal, preictal, and ictal windows, then extracting features such as spectral power, entropy, and connectivity measures. Models range from logistic regression and support vector machines on handcrafted features to convolutional and recurrent neural networks that learn directly from raw or filtered signals. Patient specific models are common because seizure patterns vary widely between individuals, so training often uses a leave one patient out or personalized fine tuning approach. Validation is done with chronological splits to avoid leaking future data into training.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on false alarms, missed seizures, and the burden of continuous monitoring, as well as data privacy for long term brain recordings. Regulatory pathways treat these systems as medical devices, and any claim of clinical benefit requires prospective evidence rather than retrospective accuracy alone. The site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, though none are specific to seizure prediction, and 210 compliance and regulation pages relevant to medical AI. Provenance of training data matters because models trained on short inpatient stays may not generalize to home environments.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward closed loop systems that couple prediction with intervention, such as responsive neurostimulation or fast acting drug delivery. Multimodal inputs, including heart rate, motion, and sleep stage, are being added to improve robustness outside the hospital. Prospective, blinded trials remain the main hurdle before routine clinical use, and regulatory frameworks for adaptive algorithms are still being worked out. Over time, seizure prediction may become one component of broader neurological forecasting tools rather than a standalone product.
